BLOCKING — two lookalike values are outside the enum. `unpleasant` (dogwood) is not a member; the schema's third tier is `unpalatable`. `harmless` (viburnum) has no member at all — the type is deadly | toxic | unpalatable only. Both need recoding, and the viburnum row ("nannyberry and blackhaw are good eating") has no honest home in this enum, so it should be recoded `unpalatable` or dropped.

BLOCKING — poison sumac (Toxicodendron vernix) is missing, and it is the one serious hazard that shares both the habitat and the growth form. NC State's toolbox rates it a high-severity poison and notes smoke from burning it can be fatal; it is a woody shrub-to-small-tree of "bogs, marshes, swamps, and thickets along river banks" — the exact wet seam this entry sends people into — with pinnately compound leaves of 7-13 leaflets and smooth bark bearing conspicuous lenticels. That last point is sharp: the entry uses "smooth stems with raised lenticels" as a positive elder confirmer in the Aralia comparison, and poison sumac has the same cue. The entry already sets the precedent for contact-only hazards by including giant hogweed and cow parsnip, and it puts the reader's hands inside the shrub with snips twice a season. The tell is clean: poison sumac's leaves are ALTERNATE with ENTIRE untoothed margins on a red rachis, and its yellowish-white drupes hang in drooping axillary panicles, against elder's OPPOSITE sharply toothed leaflets and one terminal flat black cyme.

BLOCKING — the cooking step has no duration. Step (3) says "bring the fruit to a full rolling boil and hold it there," which a reader can satisfy by touching a boil and pulling the pot. UMN Extension gives a usable number: "Boil the elderberries for at least 10 minutes." For an entry that correctly makes cooking mandatory, leaving the time unstated undercuts the whole instruction.

BLOCKING — terrain is miscoded in both directions. `upland` is defined in foraging.ts as "dry rocky slopes, barrens, pine and oak scrub" and TERRAIN_LABEL files it under "Dry slopes & barrens" — flatly contradicting the entry's own opening ("The wet seam in the landscape") and its statement that in the arid Southwest and Great Basin it is "confined almost entirely to watercourses, seeps and shaded canyon bottoms." Conversely `meadow` ("open field, old pasture, roadside verge") is absent even though the habitat text is built on roadside swales, ditch banks, fencerows, seepy field corners and wet meadow margins. Drop `upland`, add `meadow`.

The schema has no finer control, so this is not fixable by re-coding, but one clause in the habitat paragraph naming Alaska and Hawaii as outside the range would close it.

NON-BLOCKING — two toxicity claims are stated more confidently than the literature supports: Virginia creeper ("children have died from eating it") and privet ("have killed livestock and children") both rest on old and disputed case reports. Both err toward caution, so neither endangers a reader, but a guide that elsewhere flags contested taxonomy should hedge these too.

NON-BLOCKING but worth a clause — the entry directs raw flower preparations (infused sugar, vinegar, cordial) with no comment on the flowers themselves. Sources genuinely conflict: most treat flowers as the one part safe raw, while UMN Extension lists flowers among the parts carrying the cyanogenic compounds and says even dehydrated elderflowers should be heat-treated before consumption. I am not blocking on this because mainstream practice is on the entry's side, but the disagreement deserves a sentence rather than silence.
